newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore, Malaysia locked in love-hate embrace.
newsitem.headline: Singapore, Malaysia locked in love-hate embrace.

text.p: Three decades after their divorce, Singapore and Malaysia are still locked in a love-hate embrace despite ever stronger interdependence.
The latent tension was underscored this week by the howls of protest across Malaysia over disparaging remarks by Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew about the Malaysian state of Johor.
Lee outraged Malaysians by describing Johor, just across the Johor Strait from Singapore, as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".

After a day of protests in which Malaysian youths hurled insults at the former Singapore prime minister and Malaysia demanded a retraction, Lee's office said late on Thursday he apologised "unreservedly" for the offence he had caused to the government and people of Malaysia.
Political analysts said on Friday they expected the spat to die down following Lee's apology and that growing economic ties should gradually lead to more trust on both sides.
But they said similar incidents were likely to recur because of long-standing cultural conflicts and some new economic ones.

"Singapore and Malaysia have a love-hate relationship," said Naranyan Ganesan, senior political science lecturer at the National University of Singapore. "They have a symbiotic, trading partnership, but there has always been a latent tension... which is both cultural and economic."

Lee's remarks about Johor were made in a deposition in one of 13 libel lawsuits brought against Singapore opposition politician Tang Liang Hong after elections in January. Tang fled to Johor, saying he had received death threats in Singapore. Lee questioned whether Tang would be safer in Johor.
No one in Singapore is saying precisely why Lee apologised to Malaysia, but trade could be the reason.

As the row bubbled on Thursday, Singapore shares fell on fears Malaysia might retaliate economically, as it has done in the past against Britain over political rows, including a "buy British last" policy.
"If he doesn't backtrack, it's going to cost us a lot," said one dealer before Lee apologised.
Born from the same British imperial legacy and united briefly from 1963 to 1965, the two countries have followed a similar path to economic development and share many assets.

Malaysia supplies Singapore with raw materials and most of its water. Singapore's port and financial markets give Malaysian products access to world markets, although Malaysia is building up its ports in competition.
Singapore is the biggest investor in Malaysia, its biggest trading partner with two-way trade worth US$3.74 billion in January this year. But they are deeply divided culturally.
Singapore is overwhelmingly Chinese with a large Malay minority. Malays are the dominant group in Malaysia but Chinese and Indians make up nearly 40 percent of the population.
Singapore left the Malaysian Federation in 1965 partly in opposition to Malaysia's policy of preferential treatment for Malays to help them compete in an economy dominated by Chinese.
Lee raised Malaysian hackles in 1996, saying this policy was still an obstacle if the two countries were ever to reunite.
Meritocratic Singapore could never accept such discimination, he said.
Upset by what they saw as Lee's condescension, Malaysians said it was proof Singaporeans thought they were superior.
Taunting Lee, whose People's Action Party has run Singapore with an iron grip since 1959, Malaysians countered by saying at least they were democratic and allowed freedom of speech.
Economics is also helping to spin out the political rivalry.
For long the biggest shipping, financial and high-tech manufacturing centre in Southeast Asia, Singapore is gradually being overhauled by its northern neighbour.
Malaysia is now enjoying growth of more than eight percent, against around seven percent for Singapore last year, and its infrastructure is improving rapidily.
When the boss of computer software giant Microsoft, Bill Gates, decided to set up a major multimedia centre in Asia, he chose Malaysia, not Singapore.
But analysts say the growing economic interdependence and wealth on both sides of the causeway linking the two countries will eventually outweigh the differences.
Chee Soon Juan, head of the opposition Singapore Democratic Party, said the level of interdependence will rise over time.
"Who knows, eventually they may reunite -- if not politically then in some form of economic union."
